topic: Automated plan/spec completeness assurance: traceability, ambiguity detection, design-by-contract, hazard analysis, scenario coverage, and competitive planning systems
research_questions: How do requirements traceability, design-by-contract, hazard analysis, ambiguity detection, and scenario coverage systems assure plan or specification completeness?
Which official standards and mature planning or verification systems detect missing acceptance criteria, hidden assumptions, and negative-space gaps?
How can evidence links distinguish supported completeness claims, analyst inferences, and unresolved no-evidence areas?
What reusable assurance gates should Puppet Master apply before a plan is considered implementation-ready?

sources.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 - Systems and software engineering - Life cycle processes - Requirements engineering
sources.material_relevance: Defines requirements-engineering processes across the life cycle and specifies required information items, their contents, and format guidance, providing a standards baseline for plan/spec completeness.

sources.title: Appendix C: How to Write a Good Requirement
sources.material_relevance: Provides checklists for clarity, ambiguity, completeness, assumptions, traceability, correctness, interfaces, reliability, safety/security, and testability, including explicit negative-space categories.

sources.title: SWE-051 - Software Requirements Analysis
sources.material_relevance: Requires analysis of flowed-down and derived requirements for correctness, consistency, clarity, completeness, feasibility, verifiability, traceability, scenarios, assumptions, and absence of unnecessary requirements.

sources.title: SWE-052 - Bidirectional Traceability
sources.material_relevance: Specifies links across higher-level requirements, software requirements, design, code, tests, nonconformances, and hazards; calls out missing, circular, disconnected, orphan, and extra behavior as assurance findings.

sources.title: SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.material_relevance: Applies systems-security engineering throughout the life cycle and connects security requirements, risk assessment, specifications, verification, validation, and evidence to trustworthy-system assurance.

sources.title: OMG System Modeling Language Specification Version 2.0
sources.material_relevance: Defines a model-based systems language covering requirements, structure, behavior, analysis, and verification, enabling typed relationships and consistency checks across system views.

sources.title: ET: Design by Contract (tm), Assertions and Exceptions
sources.material_relevance: Documents preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants as precise specifications that can support documentation, testing, and runtime assertion monitoring.

sources.title: Gherkin Reference
sources.material_relevance: Defines executable scenario structure using Given, When, Then, And, and But steps, providing a concrete pattern for acceptance criteria and scenario coverage.

sources.title: Overview of DOORS Next
sources.material_relevance: Describes a commercial requirements system with typed links, suspect-link change impact, requirements-to-test coverage metrics, baselines, configuration management, reviews, and history.

sources.title: Doorstop: Requirements management using version control
sources.material_relevance: Stores requirements and test cases as versioned YAML items, organizes documents into a traceable hierarchy, validates the tree, and publishes reports.

sources.title: OpenFastTrace: Open source requirement tracing suite
sources.material_relevance: Provides requirement tracing intended to show whether planned specification items were implemented and to identify obsolete product parts, with HTML reporting and build integration.

sources.title: Automated Smell Detection and Recommendation in Natural Language Requirements
sources.material_relevance: Primary research on Paska, an NLP tool that detects requirement smells and recommends controlled-natural-language improvements; the reported industrial evaluation supports review assistance, not automatic completeness certification.

findings.claim: Requirements completeness is treated as a lifecycle information-quality problem plus coverage of downstream assurance artifacts, not as prose quality alone.
findings.notes: ISO 29148 frames requirements engineering as defined processes and information items; NASA adds quality dimensions, assumptions, traceability, scenarios, and verification readiness.

findings.claim: A negative-space completeness review should explicitly check functional, performance, interface, environment, facility, transport, training, personnel, operability, safety, security, appearance, physical, and design concerns rather than infer coverage from feature prose.
findings.notes: NASA's validation checklist directly enumerates these overlooked requirement areas and separately requires assumptions to be stated.

findings.claim: Bidirectional traceability can detect both missing coverage and unjustified scope: parent-to-child flowdown, downstream implementation/verification links, orphan or disconnected elements, circular links, and extra behavior are distinct checks.
findings.notes: NASA explicitly calls for parent and lower-level links and gap analysis; Doorstop demonstrates a version-controlled hierarchical validator pattern.

findings.claim: Hazards and risk controls need their own traceability path through requirements and verification evidence; ordinary requirement-to-test coverage does not establish hazard mitigation by itself.
findings.notes: NASA calls out hazard-to-requirement-to-test links and objective evidence; NIST makes risk, security requirements, verification, and validation lifecycle concerns.

findings.claim: Change assurance requires invalidating or flagging affected links and preserving a versioned baseline, rather than relying on a one-time completeness review.
findings.notes: DOORS Next describes suspect links, baselines, configuration management, and history; NASA requires maintained bidirectional traceability.

findings.claim: Model-based assurance can make requirements, behavior, analysis, and verification cases explicit and related, but the model still needs project-specific practices and evidence to establish completeness.
findings.notes: OMG describes SysML v2's coverage of requirements, behavior, structure, analysis, and verification and its emphasis on consistency and traceability; the limit about project-specific evidence is an analytical qualification.

findings.claim: Design-by-contract supplies a reusable way to turn hidden assumptions into explicit preconditions, guarantees into postconditions, and stable state expectations into invariants that can be checked or reviewed.
findings.notes: The Eiffel documentation defines the three contract categories and their use in specification, documentation, testing, and runtime assertion monitoring.

findings.claim: Executable scenario patterns make acceptance criteria operational by representing preconditions, actions, and observable outcomes in an ordered, typed form.
findings.notes: Cucumber defines Given/When/Then execution; NASA requires review against nominal and off-nominal operational scenarios and a feasible verification method.

findings.claim: Mature lightweight tools show that traceability assurance can run in version control and CI: Doorstop validates a requirement tree, while OpenFastTrace reports planned-versus-implemented coverage and obsolete parts.
findings.notes: Both project repositories describe direct repository/build workflows and report generation; they demonstrate implementation patterns rather than a universal process standard.

findings.claim: Automated requirement-smell detection is a useful review aid, but evidence for quality-detector performance is tied to particular smell definitions, datasets, domains, and evaluation setups.
findings.notes: The Paska paper reports an industrial case study and precision/recall results for its defined smells and recommendations; those results do not establish universal completeness detection.

findings.claim: The cross-source pattern is layered assurance rather than a single completeness score: quality checks, typed trace coverage, scenario or contract checks, hazard/risk evidence, and change-controlled baselines each cover different failure surfaces.
findings.notes: This is a synthesis across the sources; no one source specifies the exact layered architecture or a universal score.

findings.claim: No reviewed source proves that an LLM-only plan review can reliably discover all negative-space gaps or certify implementation readiness without domain review and executable evidence.
findings.notes: The reviewed sources describe human checklists, typed links, formal or executable checks, and bounded smell-detector evaluations; none establishes the stronger LLM-only guarantee.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: A checklist rubric tests requirement wording, ambiguity, assumptions, completeness categories, correctness, consistency, traceability, interfaces, reliability, and verifiability.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A plan assurance system should expose named dimensions and failed checks rather than only a pass/fail summary.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: A typed, bidirectional trace graph connects higher-level needs to derived requirements, design/implementation artifacts, verification artifacts, nonconformances, and hazards.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Completeness gates should check required edge types in both directions and identify orphan, extra, circular, and disconnected nodes.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Requirements analysis checks parent flowdown, derived requirements, scenario coverage, assumptions, feasibility, verifiability, and absence of unnecessary requirements before design begins.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A plan gate should include both missing-content and unjustified-content findings.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Commercial requirements management combines trace links, impact analysis, suspect-link status, review workflows, coverage metrics, baselines, and configuration history.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Change state and evidence freshness are first-class assurance data, not merely metadata on the source paragraph.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Model-based systems engineering represents requirements, structure, behavior, analysis, and verification in a consistent, traceable model.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A plan system can borrow typed model relations without requiring every plan to become a full SysML model.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Design by Contract expresses component expectations and guarantees as preconditions, postconditions, and invariants that can be checked during development or execution.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: High-risk plan assumptions and invariants can be promoted to executable or reviewable contracts.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: BDD tooling uses Given/When/Then scenarios as ordered acceptance criteria whose steps are executable through matching definitions.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Scenario coverage can be represented as structured evidence rather than free-text examples.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Text-first open-source tools keep requirement items in version control, validate trace links, and publish machine-readable or HTML reports as part of repository workflows.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A lightweight assurance lane can provide useful governance without requiring a centralized commercial repository.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: A layered assurance stack can combine linguistic smell detection, typed traceability, executable scenarios/contracts, hazard evidence, and immutable baselines.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: The layers should produce separate findings and evidence links so a strong result in one layer cannot hide a gap in another.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Ambiguous, vague, indefinite, compound, or unverifiable wording is accepted as a requirement without a measurable interpretation.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Run lexical and structural checks, require one clear thought per requirement, reject indefinite terms, and require a verification method and success criteria.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The plan omits entire requirement dimensions or hides unresolved values and assumptions without a disposition path.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use a negative-space matrix, explicit TBD/TBR tracking, named assumption owners, and a required rationale for deliberate N/A decisions.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The trace graph contains missing, circular, disconnected, orphan, or extra nodes, so a green document review masks incomplete or unjustified scope.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Validate edge cardinality and direction, report orphan and extra behavior separately, and fail or quarantine unresolved graph defects.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Hazards or security risks are documented separately from requirements and tests, leaving mitigation claims without end-to-end evidence.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Require hazard/risk to control, requirement, verification, and residual-risk links, with objective evidence and explicit disposition of gaps.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A requirement changes after downstream artifacts were reviewed, but stale links and affected tests or designs are not revalidated.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Propagate suspect status from changed nodes, require review of affected edges, and compare against a named baseline before closing the change.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Scenario evidence covers only nominal paths while operational modes, boundaries, failure conditions, or off-nominal operator actions remain unspecified.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Require scenario families for nominal, boundary, error, recovery, and off-nominal modes and link each to an observable expected outcome.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A smell detector or ambiguity classifier is generalized beyond the vocabulary, labels, domain, or dataset on which it was evaluated.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Treat automated detections as review candidates, record detector scope and confidence, and calibrate against domain-labeled examples before using results as gates.

failure_modes.failure_mode: No reviewed source demonstrates a competitor or standard that automatically proves all negative-space categories are covered for an arbitrary plan.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Keep negative-space coverage explicit and human-adjudicable; do not infer universal coverage from a traceability percentage or an NLP score.

implications.implication: Treat implementation-ready as a multi-dimensional assurance state covering wording quality, trace coverage, scenarios or contracts, hazard/risk/assumption disposition, and evidence freshness.
implications.rationale: The sources cover different assurance surfaces; a single binary prose review would not represent all of them.

implications.implication: Represent plan items and assurance artifacts as typed nodes and links with explicit required incoming and outgoing edge classes.
implications.rationale: NASA and IBM show the value of typed lifecycle links, while Doorstop demonstrates a lightweight hierarchical validation implementation.

implications.implication: Add a reusable completeness matrix over functional, performance, interface, environment, operations, safety, security, reliability, maintainability, training, personnel, and physical concerns, with explicit N/A rationale.
implications.rationale: NASA's checklist supplies a concrete negative-space taxonomy; the matrix form is a proposed reusable implementation for Puppet Master.

implications.implication: Make evidence provenance and evidence class visible at claim level, separating source-supported claims, analyst inferences, and unresolved no-evidence areas.
implications.rationale: NIST and NASA emphasize traceable objective evidence; the three-class presentation is an assurance design inference, not a direct mandate from either source.

implications.implication: Propagate a suspect or stale state through the plan graph whenever a requirement, assumption, hazard, scenario, or verification artifact changes.
implications.rationale: This adapts IBM's suspect-link and baseline pattern to the broader plan assurance graph.

implications.implication: Provide a lightweight text/version-control assurance lane for every plan and an optional formal contract or model-check lane for critical or high-risk plans.
implications.rationale: The sources show complementary cost and rigor profiles; the lane split is proposed for proportional assurance.

implications.implication: Do not make a single numerical completeness score the sole release gate.
implications.rationale: No reviewed source defines a domain-independent score that safely substitutes for typed traceability, scenario evidence, risk disposition, and review judgment.

novel_ideas.idea: Negative-space coverage lattice: render scope dimensions as rows and plan sections, links, evidence, and dispositions as columns; require every cell to be covered or explicitly marked N/A with rationale.
novel_ideas.rationale: This turns NASA's enumerated overlooked areas into a repeatable gap-detection surface.

novel_ideas.idea: Assumption-to-contract compiler: translate an assumption into a precondition, a promised outcome into a postcondition, and a stable state rule into an invariant; mark items that cannot be made executable as review-only obligations.
novel_ideas.rationale: This combines Eiffel contract categories with NASA's requirement-rationale and assumption checks.

novel_ideas.idea: Evidence-class ledger: attach supported_claim, inference, or no_evidence to each assurance claim and require direct source or executable-receipt mappings for supported claims.
novel_ideas.rationale: The sources require traceable objective evidence; the explicit evidence taxonomy is a proposed reporting mechanism.

novel_ideas.idea: Change-suspect propagation: when a plan atom changes, automatically mark downstream scenarios, contracts, risks, hazards, and verification links as suspect until revalidated.
novel_ideas.rationale: This extends commercial suspect-link behavior to the full plan assurance surface.

novel_ideas.idea: Scenario cross-product sampler: derive candidate scenarios across nominal/off-nominal modes, roles, boundaries, dependency failures, retries, and recovery, then require each accepted scenario to map to an observable outcome.
novel_ideas.rationale: NASA supplies the nominal/off-nominal review requirement and Cucumber supplies a structured executable scenario form; the cross-product generator is novel.

novel_ideas.idea: Two-pass smell assurance: let automated smell detection propose ambiguity or quality findings, then require a domain reviewer to resolve each finding and record the accepted wording or rationale.
novel_ideas.rationale: Paska demonstrates automated detection and recommendation; NASA's checklist supplies the human validation dimensions.

novel_ideas.idea: No reviewed source demonstrates that a general-purpose LLM can safely auto-promote an arbitrary plan to implementation-ready using text alone.
novel_ideas.rationale: This is an explicit research boundary, not a product claim; the reviewed evidence supports assistive detection and layered verification instead.

unresolved_questions.question: What quantitative coverage thresholds, if any, are appropriate for different plan risk classes and domains without turning the metric into a false proof of completeness?
How should ambiguity and requirement-smell detectors be validated across domain vocabulary, terminology, languages, and document styles?
Which plan classes should require executable contracts or formal model checks, and what evidence is sufficient when a requirement cannot be expressed executable?
How should unknown, TBD, TBR, and deliberate N/A states be represented and aged so that unresolved gaps cannot be hidden by status changes?
What is the minimum hazard, risk, or security evidence required when a plan has no applicable external safety standard but still has consequential failure modes?
How should Puppet Master measure reviewer burden, detector false positives, and time-to-resolution for automated ambiguity or smell findings?
How should typed trace semantics and evidence provenance be preserved when plan artifacts cross tools or repositories with different link models and baselines?
